title: Lacunar infarcts and the lenticulostriate arteries
text:
The lateral striate (lenticulostriate) arteries leave the M1 segment of the middle cerebral artery at right angles as small end arteries supplying the lentiform nucleus, caudate and internal capsule. Chronic hypertension and diabetes cause lipohyalinosis and occlusion, producing small deep infarcts under 15 mm (lacunes).
The classic lacunar syndromes have NO cortical signs (no aphasia, neglect, visual field defect or impaired consciousness): pure motor hemiparesis of face, arm and leg (posterior limb of the internal capsule or basis pontis); pure sensory stroke (ventral posterolateral thalamus); sensorimotor stroke (thalamocapsular); ataxic hemiparesis (pons or internal capsule); and dysarthria-clumsy hand (pons or genu of the internal capsule). Because the capsule packs all descending fibres into a small space, a tiny lacune can cause dense hemiplegia. Multiple lacunes cause vascular dementia and a shuffling 'marche à petits pas' gait.

title: Posterior cerebral artery stroke
text:
The posterior cerebral artery supplies the occipital lobe, the inferomedial temporal lobe (including the hippocampus), the splenium of the corpus callosum and, through its perforators, the thalamus and midbrain. Occlusion (usually embolic, often from the top of the basilar artery) causes a contralateral homonymous hemianopia, frequently with macular sparing because the occipital pole also receives middle cerebral collaterals.
Dominant (left) PCA infarction involving the splenium produces alexia without agraphia: the patient can write but cannot read what they wrote, because visual information from the intact right occipital cortex cannot cross to the left language areas. Bilateral PCA infarction causes cortical blindness, sometimes with denial of blindness (Anton syndrome), and memory loss from bilateral hippocampal damage. Perforator involvement adds thalamic sensory loss or a Weber-type midbrain syndrome.

title: Anterior communicating artery aneurysm
text:
The anterior communicating artery complex is the commonest site of intracranial berry aneurysm (about a third). Rupture causes subarachnoid haemorrhage, sometimes with blood in the interhemispheric fissure or gyrus rectus. Because the complex sits above the optic chiasm, a large unruptured aneurysm compresses the chiasm from above, producing a bitemporal field defect that starts inferiorly (a pituitary tumour, pressing from below, starts superiorly).
Small perforators from the anterior communicating artery supply the basal forebrain (septal nuclei and cholinergic nucleus basalis of Meynert), anterior hypothalamus and fornix. After rupture or clipping, damage here causes the 'ACoA syndrome': anterograde amnesia, confabulation and apathy or disinhibition. Vasospasm in both anterior cerebral arteries can additionally cause bilateral leg weakness and abulia.

title: Subarachnoid haemorrhage: diagnosis and complications
text:
About 85% of non-traumatic subarachnoid haemorrhages come from ruptured berry aneurysms of the circle of Willis; perimesencephalic bleeds and arteriovenous malformations account for most of the rest. The typical story is a thunderclap headache reaching maximum within a minute, often with vomiting, neck stiffness (meningism), photophobia, seizures or collapse; a sentinel headache may precede it.
Non-contrast CT within 6 hours of onset is almost 100% sensitive. After that, lumbar puncture at least 12 hours after onset looks for xanthochromia (bilirubin from lysed red cells), which distinguishes true haemorrhage from a traumatic tap. The aneurysm is secured by endovascular coiling or clipping.
Complications: rebleeding (highest in the first 24 hours), vasospasm with delayed cerebral ischaemia from day 4 to 14 (oral nimodipine reduces poor outcome), communicating hydrocephalus from blocked arachnoid granulations, and hyponatraemia from cerebral salt wasting or SIADH.

targets: Lateral pontine branches of basilar artery
title: Lateral pontine (AICA) syndrome
text:
Occlusion of the anterior inferior cerebellar artery infarcts the lateral caudal pons and the inferior cerebellum. The picture resembles the lateral medullary syndrome: ipsilateral loss of facial pain and temperature (spinal trigeminal nucleus and tract), ipsilateral Horner syndrome, ipsilateral limb ataxia (middle cerebellar peduncle) and contralateral loss of pain and temperature in the body (lateral spinothalamic tract), with vertigo and nystagmus.
Two features distinguish it from a PICA infarct: an ipsilateral lower motor neurone facial palsy (facial nucleus in the pons) and sudden ipsilateral deafness and tinnitus, because the labyrinthine artery to the inner ear usually arises from AICA. Sudden hearing loss with vertigo in a vascular patient should raise this possibility rather than a purely peripheral cause.

targets: Medial pontine branches of basilar artery
title: Ventral pontine syndromes: Millard-Gubler and Foville
text:
Paramedian branches of the basilar artery supply the ventral pons, where the corticospinal fibres run close to the fascicles of the abducens and facial nerves. This produces crossed signs, the hallmark of a brainstem lesion: cranial nerve palsy on the side of the lesion with hemiparesis of the opposite limbs.
Millard-Gubler syndrome: ipsilateral lateral rectus palsy (VI) and lower motor neurone facial palsy (VII) with contralateral hemiparesis. Foville syndrome adds ipsilateral horizontal gaze palsy when the abducens nucleus or paramedian pontine reticular formation is involved. Bilateral ventral pontine infarction from basilar occlusion causes the locked-in syndrome, with only vertical eye movements and blinking preserved.

title: Superior cerebellar artery: infarction and microvascular decompression
text:
The superior cerebellar artery arises near the top of the basilar artery, winds around the midbrain just below the oculomotor nerve and supplies the superior cerebellar hemisphere, vermis, dentate nucleus and superior cerebellar peduncle. Infarction causes ipsilateral limb ataxia and intention tremor, dysarthria and gait ataxia, sometimes with contralateral pain and temperature loss.
A looping superior cerebellar artery compressing the trigeminal sensory root at its entry zone into the pons is the usual cause of classical trigeminal neuralgia. When carbamazepine fails, microvascular decompression (Jannetta procedure) through a retrosigmoid craniotomy separates the artery from the nerve with a Teflon pad and gives the most durable relief; percutaneous ablation at the trigeminal ganglion or stereotactic radiosurgery are alternatives for frail patients. Compression of the facial nerve root by AICA causes hemifacial spasm in the same way.

title: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia and horizontal gaze palsies
text:
Horizontal gaze is organised in the pons: the paramedian pontine reticular formation drives the abducens nucleus, which contains motor neurones to the ipsilateral lateral rectus and interneurones whose axons cross and ascend in the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) to the medial rectus subnucleus of the opposite oculomotor nucleus.
An MLF lesion causes internuclear ophthalmoplegia: on looking to the opposite side the eye on the side of the lesion fails to adduct and the abducting eye shows nystagmus, while convergence is preserved (it does not use the MLF). Bilateral INO in a young adult is almost diagnostic of multiple sclerosis; unilateral INO in an older patient suggests a brainstem infarct.
A lesion of the abducens NUCLEUS causes a horizontal gaze palsy to that side (both eyes), not just a lateral rectus palsy, often with a facial palsy because the facial nerve loops around the nucleus (facial colliculus). Nucleus plus adjacent MLF gives the 'one-and-a-half' syndrome: the only horizontal movement left is abduction of the opposite eye.

title: Friedreich ataxia and the spinocerebellar tracts
text:
The posterior spinocerebellar tract arises from Clarke's column (nucleus dorsalis, C8-L2) and carries unconscious proprioception from the ipsilateral lower limb through the inferior cerebellar peduncle; the anterior spinocerebellar tract crosses twice and enters via the superior peduncle. Both therefore signal to the cerebellar hemisphere on the same side as the limb.
Friedreich ataxia (autosomal recessive GAA repeat expansion in the frataxin gene) degenerates the spinocerebellar tracts, dorsal columns, corticospinal tracts and dorsal root ganglia from late childhood: progressive gait and limb ataxia, dysarthria, loss of vibration and joint position sense, absent ankle reflexes with EXTENSOR plantar responses (a classic combination), pes cavus and scoliosis. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is the main cause of death, and diabetes mellitus is common. Sensory (dorsal column) ataxia worsens with eyes closed (positive Romberg test); cerebellar ataxia does not.

title: Upper versus lower motor neurone lesions
text:
About 85 to 90% of corticospinal fibres cross in the pyramidal decussation at the medulla-cord junction to form the lateral corticospinal tract; the uncrossed remainder descends in the anterior corticospinal tract to axial muscles. Lesions above the decussation weaken the opposite side; lesions in the cord weaken the same side.
Upper motor neurone lesions give spasticity with 'clasp-knife' tone, hyperreflexia, clonus, an extensor plantar (Babinski) response, little wasting, and a pyramidal pattern of weakness (arm extensors and leg flexors weaker, hence the hemiplegic posture of a flexed arm and extended leg). In the acute phase of stroke or cord injury the limbs are flaccid and areflexic (spinal or cerebral shock).
Lower motor neurone lesions (anterior horn, root, plexus, nerve) give flaccid weakness in the distribution of the root or nerve, wasting, fasciculations and reduced or absent reflexes. Motor neurone disease characteristically mixes both.

title: Decorticate and decerebrate posturing
text:
The red nucleus (via the rubrospinal tract) facilitates upper limb flexors, while the lateral vestibulospinal and pontine reticulospinal tracts drive antigravity extensors; the cortex normally inhibits both.
Decorticate posturing (flexion of the arms and wrists with extended legs, GCS motor score 3) follows lesions ABOVE the red nucleus, in the hemispheres, internal capsule or thalamus, where rubrospinal flexor drive to the arms survives. Decerebrate posturing (extension and internal rotation of arms and legs with clenched jaw, GCS motor score 2) follows lesions between the red nucleus and the vestibular nuclei, in the midbrain or upper pons, leaving unopposed vestibulospinal and reticulospinal extensor tone. A change from decorticate to decerebrate posturing indicates rostrocaudal progression of transtentorial herniation and a worse prognosis.

title: Anterior spinal artery and the artery of Adamkiewicz
text:
The single anterior spinal artery, formed from both vertebral arteries, supplies the anterior two-thirds of the cord (anterior horns, spinothalamic and corticospinal tracts); the paired posterior spinal arteries supply the dorsal columns. Below the cervical cord the anterior spinal artery depends on segmental radiculomedullary feeders. The largest, the great anterior radiculomedullary artery of Adamkiewicz, usually arises from a LEFT posterior intercostal or lumbar artery between T9 and T12 and supplies the lower two-thirds of the cord.
Occlusion or sacrifice of this artery during thoracoabdominal aneurysm repair, endovascular stenting, aortic dissection or embolisation causes anterior cord syndrome: flaccid then spastic paraplegia, a sensory level for pain and temperature and loss of sphincter control, with preserved vibration and proprioception. The mid-thoracic cord (about T4-T8) is a watershed zone vulnerable to hypotension. Lumbar CSF drainage during aortic surgery lowers the risk by improving cord perfusion pressure.

title: Autonomic dysreflexia and neurogenic shock
text:
Sympathetic preganglionic neurones lie in the intermediolateral cell column from T1 to L2; the large splanchnic outflow to the gut vessels leaves from about T5 to T12.
Autonomic dysreflexia occurs in patients with chronic cord injuries at or above T6. A noxious stimulus below the lesion, most often a blocked catheter, full bladder or constipation, triggers a massive reflex sympathetic discharge that the brain cannot inhibit: severe paroxysmal hypertension, pounding headache, and flushing and sweating ABOVE the level of injury, with reflex bradycardia via the baroreceptors and vagus. It is an emergency (stroke, seizures): sit the patient up, loosen clothing, find and remove the trigger (catheterise), and give a rapid-acting antihypertensive if needed.
In contrast, neurogenic shock after an acute high cord injury is loss of sympathetic tone: hypotension with bradycardia and warm peripheries.

title: Lumbar puncture, spinal and epidural anaesthesia
text:
Tuffier's line between the top of the iliac crests crosses the L4 spinous process or L4/5 interspace; the needle is passed below the conus (L1/L2) with the patient curled to open the interlaminar spaces. It traverses skin, subcutaneous fat, supraspinous ligament, interspinous ligament and ligamentum flavum (a distinct resistance) into the epidural space, then the dura and arachnoid into the CSF of the lumbar cistern.
Epidural anaesthesia stops in the epidural space (fat and the valveless internal vertebral venous plexus), found by loss of resistance to saline or air; a catheter allows continuous labour analgesia. Spinal anaesthesia injects a small dose into the CSF for a rapid dense block; too much or a head-down tilt gives a high spinal with hypotension, bradycardia and respiratory failure.
Complications: post-dural puncture headache (worse upright, eased lying flat, less with fine pencil-point needles, treated with an epidural blood patch), epidural haematoma in anticoagulated patients (compressive cord or cauda signs) and infection. Lumbar puncture is contraindicated with signs of raised intracranial pressure from a mass (risk of coning).

title: Wernicke encephalopathy and the Papez circuit
text:
Thiamine deficiency (alcohol dependence, hyperemesis gravidarum, bariatric surgery, refeeding) damages the mamillary bodies, medial thalamus and periaqueductal grey. Wernicke encephalopathy is the triad of confusion, ophthalmoplegia (often lateral rectus palsy or nystagmus) and ataxia, although the full triad is present in a minority. Intravenous thiamine must be given before glucose, because glucose metabolism consumes the remaining thiamine. MRI shows mamillary body swelling and later atrophy.
Untreated, it progresses to Korsakoff syndrome: dense anterograde and patchy retrograde amnesia with confabulation and preserved intellect. The mamillary bodies are a relay in the Papez circuit (hippocampus to fornix to mamillary body, mamillothalamic tract to the anterior thalamic nucleus, then cingulate gyrus and back to the hippocampus), so damage anywhere along it impairs the formation of new memories.

title: Parasagittal lesions: the paracentral lobule
text:
The paracentral lobule on the medial surface of the hemisphere contains the motor and sensory cortex for the contralateral leg and foot and the cortical centre that inhibits micturition. It is supplied by the anterior cerebral artery.
A parasagittal meningioma arising from the falx can compress both paracentral lobules, producing a spastic paraparesis with urinary incontinence and no sensory level: a picture easily mistaken for a spinal cord lesion, so imaging of the head is needed when a cord MRI is normal. Unilateral lesions (ACA infarcts, parasagittal tumours) cause weakness and cortical sensory loss of the opposite leg with relative sparing of the arm and face, and focal motor seizures may start in the foot (Jacksonian march).

title: Conduction aphasia and ideomotor apraxia
text:
The arcuate fasciculus runs deep to the supramarginal gyrus, connecting Wernicke's area to Broca's area. A dominant supramarginal lesion causes conduction aphasia: fluent speech with phonemic paraphasias and good comprehension but strikingly poor REPETITION, as the patient understands but cannot relay what was heard.
Other aphasias sort by repetition. Global aphasia (large MCA infarct) impairs all functions. Transcortical aphasias spare repetition because the perisylvian loop is intact and the lesion lies in the watershed zone around it: transcortical motor (anterior, non-fluent) or transcortical sensory (posterior, fluent with poor comprehension).
The dominant inferior parietal lobule also stores learned motor programmes: lesions cause ideomotor apraxia, inability to mime actions on command (waving, using a comb) despite normal strength and comprehension. Angular gyrus lesions add alexia with agraphia and the Gerstmann tetrad.

title: Central auditory pathway lesions
text:
Sound travels from the cochlear nuclei to both superior olivary complexes, up the lateral lemnisci to the inferior colliculi, then to the medial geniculate bodies and the primary auditory cortex in the transverse temporal gyri of Heschl. Because each ear projects bilaterally above the cochlear nuclei, a unilateral lesion of the lemniscus, colliculus, geniculate body or auditory cortex does NOT cause deafness in one ear; unilateral hearing loss localises to the ear, the cochlear nerve or the cochlear nuclei.
Bilateral temporal lesions cause cortical deafness or pure word deafness (sounds are heard but speech cannot be understood). Irritative lesions of the auditory cortex cause auditory auras and hallucinations in temporal lobe epilepsy. Brainstem auditory evoked responses test each relay station: wave I (cochlear nerve), III (superior olive region) and V (inferior colliculus region); a prolonged I-V interval suggests a vestibular schwannoma or demyelination.

title: Anosmia, olfactory groove meningioma and orbitofrontal damage
text:
Olfactory nerve fibres pass through the cribriform plate of the ethmoid to the olfactory bulb lying on the gyrus rectus. Frontal head injury shears these fibres (anosmia in up to a quarter of serious head injuries) and cribriform plate fractures cause CSF rhinorrhoea (positive for beta-2 transferrin) with a risk of meningitis. Anosmia is also an early feature of Parkinson disease, follows viral infections including COVID-19, and with hypogonadotropic hypogonadism indicates Kallmann syndrome (failed migration of GnRH neurones alongside the olfactory placode).
An olfactory groove meningioma grows silently beneath the frontal lobes, causing unilateral anosmia, apathy or disinhibition, and the Foster Kennedy syndrome: ipsilateral optic atrophy from direct compression with contralateral papilloedema from raised pressure. Orbitofrontal damage (trauma, frontotemporal dementia) causes disinhibition, impulsivity and poor social judgement with preserved intelligence, as famously in Phineas Gage.

title: Aqueduct stenosis and endoscopic third ventriculostomy
text:
The cerebral aqueduct is the narrowest part of the ventricular system, so it is the commonest site of obstructive hydrocephalus. Causes: congenital stenosis (including X-linked L1CAM mutations with adducted thumbs), tectal plate glioma, pineal tumours, and scarring after haemorrhage or meningitis. Imaging shows dilated lateral and third ventricles with a normal-sized fourth ventricle, localising the block.
Infants present with an enlarging head, bulging fontanelle, 'sunsetting' eyes (upgaze palsy from pressure on the dorsal midbrain) and dilated scalp veins; older patients with headache worse in the morning, vomiting and papilloedema.
Besides a ventriculoperitoneal shunt, obstructive hydrocephalus can be treated by endoscopic third ventriculostomy: a hole is made in the floor of the third ventricle between the mamillary bodies and the infundibular recess, letting CSF bypass the aqueduct into the interpeduncular cistern. The basilar artery lies just beneath and is the main hazard.

title: Deep venous thrombosis and vein of Galen malformation
text:
The internal cerebral veins drain the thalami, basal ganglia and deep white matter into the great cerebral vein of Galen, which joins the inferior sagittal sinus to form the straight sinus. Thrombosis of this deep system (dehydrated infants, pregnancy, thrombophilia) causes bilateral thalamic venous infarction or haemorrhage, presenting with reduced consciousness, confusion and memory disturbance rather than focal weakness. MR or CT venography shows the missing flow; treatment is anticoagulation even when there is haemorrhage.
A vein of Galen malformation is an arteriovenous fistula into a dilated embryonic median prosencephalic vein. In neonates the huge shunt causes high-output cardiac failure; in infants, macrocephaly and hydrocephalus from venous hypertension and compression of the aqueduct. It is treated by staged endovascular embolisation.

title: Septo-optic dysplasia and cavum septi pellucidi
text:
Septo-optic dysplasia (de Morsier syndrome) combines absence of the septum pellucidum, optic nerve hypoplasia and hypothalamic-pituitary dysfunction. Children present with nystagmus and poor vision (small pale optic discs), neonatal hypoglycaemia, prolonged jaundice and micropenis from pituitary hormone deficiencies (growth hormone, ACTH, TSH, gonadotropins, sometimes diabetes insipidus). Adrenal crisis during illness is the main danger, so full endocrine assessment is essential.
A cavum septi pellucidi (a fluid space between the two leaflets) is normal in fetuses and neonates and usually closes in infancy; persistence is a normal variant but is commoner after repetitive head trauma, as in boxers with chronic traumatic encephalopathy. The septum is the midline marker on axial imaging: its shift indicates subfalcine herniation.

title: Acute vertigo: peripheral or central?
text:
Vestibular neuritis (probably viral inflammation of the vestibular nerve) causes days of severe continuous vertigo, nausea and gait unsteadiness WITHOUT hearing loss; labyrinthitis adds deafness. The key danger is a posterior circulation stroke (cerebellum, lateral medulla) that mimics it.
The HINTS examination separates them in a patient with continuous vertigo and nystagmus: Head Impulse (a corrective saccade on turning toward the affected side indicates a peripheral lesion; a NORMAL head impulse is worrying), Nystagmus (unidirectional horizontal in peripheral lesions; direction-changing, vertical or purely torsional suggests central) and Test of Skew (vertical misalignment suggests central). Any central sign, or new deafness, warrants urgent MRI.
Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo gives brief vertigo on head movement from otoconia in the posterior semicircular canal: diagnosed by the Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre and treated by the Epley repositioning manoeuvre. Flocculonodular lesions impair gaze holding and cause downbeat nystagmus (also seen with Chiari malformation).

title: Taste pathway and localising a facial nerve lesion
text:
Taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue travels in the lingual nerve, then the chorda tympani, which crosses the middle ear between the malleus and incus under the tympanic membrane to join the facial nerve in the facial canal. Taste from the posterior third and vallate papillae travels in the glossopharyngeal nerve and from the epiglottis in the vagus. All end in the rostral (gustatory) nucleus of the solitary tract, which projects to the ventral posteromedial thalamus and the insular and opercular taste cortex.
The branches of the facial nerve allow a lesion to be localised: loss of tear production (greater petrosal nerve, from the geniculate ganglion) means a lesion at or proximal to the geniculate ganglion; hyperacusis (nerve to stapedius) a lesion above the stapedius branch; loss of taste a lesion above the chorda tympani; and pure facial weakness a lesion in or beyond the stylomastoid foramen (parotid tumour, surgery). Middle ear surgery or chronic otitis can injure the chorda tympani alone, causing a metallic taste or ipsilateral ageusia.

title: Bulbar versus pseudobulbar palsy
text:
The nucleus ambiguus supplies the muscles of the palate, pharynx and larynx through the glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves (and cranial accessory), and the hypoglossal nucleus supplies the tongue. Their upper motor neurone input comes bilaterally in the corticobulbar tracts, so a single hemisphere stroke rarely causes lasting swallowing failure.
Bulbar palsy (lower motor neurone: motor neurone disease, Guillain-Barré syndrome, myasthenia, syringobulbia, brainstem stroke) gives a wasted, fasciculating tongue, nasal speech from palatal weakness, absent gag reflex, nasal regurgitation and aspiration.
Pseudobulbar palsy (bilateral upper motor neurone lesions: bilateral strokes, motor neurone disease, multiple sclerosis) gives a small spastic tongue that cannot protrude quickly, slow slurred 'hot-potato' speech, a brisk jaw jerk and emotional lability (inappropriate laughing or crying). Motor neurone disease can produce both at once. Unilateral vagal lesions deviate the uvula AWAY from the weak side.

title: Metastatic spinal cord compression
text:
Breast, lung, prostate and renal cancers and myeloma seed the vertebral bodies through the valveless vertebral venous plexus (Batson plexus); collapse or epidural tumour then compresses the cord. About 70% of cases are thoracic, where the canal is narrowest relative to the cord.
Back pain comes first, often weeks before neurological signs: thoracic pain, pain worse lying flat or on coughing, night pain and band-like radicular pain around the chest are red flags in anyone with cancer. Weakness, a sensory level, and bladder and bowel dysfunction follow; outcome depends on how well the patient walks at the time of treatment. Below L1 the same process compresses the cauda equina.
Management is an emergency: whole-spine MRI within 24 hours (multiple levels are common), high-dose dexamethasone, then decompressive surgery with stabilisation or radiotherapy.

title: Cervical cord injury: level and function
text:
The phrenic nerve arises from C3-C5 ('C3, 4, 5 keeps the diaphragm alive'), so complete injuries at C3 or above need permanent ventilation, and injuries at C4-C5 often need temporary ventilatory support as the cord swells upward. Cervical cord levels lie about one segment above the corresponding vertebra.
Key preserved function by lowest intact level: C4 shoulder shrug and diaphragm; C5 elbow flexion and shoulder abduction (biceps jerk C5-C6); C6 wrist extension, allowing a 'tenodesis grip' and independent transfers; C7 elbow extension (triceps jerk) and finger extension; C8 finger flexion; T1 small hand muscles. Injuries are classified by the ASIA impairment scale; sacral sparing (perianal sensation, voluntary anal contraction) marks an incomplete injury with better prognosis. Hyperextension of a spondylotic neck without fracture causes central cord syndrome, with arms weaker than legs.

title: Upper lumbar radiculopathy and the lumbar myotomes
text:
A posterolateral disc herniation compresses the nerve root passing to the level BELOW (an L3/4 disc compresses the L4 root), whereas a far-lateral (foraminal) herniation compresses the root exiting at that level (L3). Upper lumbar radiculopathy causes anterior thigh pain, a positive femoral stretch test (pain on knee flexion with the patient prone) rather than a positive straight leg raise, and may mimic hip or knee disease.
Myotomes to test: L2 hip flexion, L3 knee extension, L4 ankle dorsiflexion (tibialis anterior) and knee jerk (L3-L4), L5 great toe extension and hip abduction, S1 plantarflexion, eversion and ankle jerk. Sensation: L3 over the medial knee, L4 over the medial leg and medial malleolus, L5 over the dorsum of the foot and first web space, S1 the lateral foot and sole. Diabetic lumbosacral radiculoplexus neuropathy (diabetic amyotrophy) causes painful proximal thigh wasting in the same distribution.
